posts.title: The Silent Performance Killer - False Sharing in C++
posts.text: One day I ran into a weird performance issue when tunning the ring buffer module of a high performance C++ RPC framework. I cooperated with another colleague, aiming to write a fast ring buffer, somehow he updated the key struct definition, we weren’t on the same page though.Eventually the performance benchmark ended up performing poorly. In hindsight, the degradation was not directly a bug in the code, but a feature of the hardware. In our benchmark, the throughput under 2 threads was better than that of 8 threads, which was really interesting. That was caused by false sharing, one of the most counterintuitive performance bugs in concurrent C++. TL;DR False sharing occurs when multiple threads access and modify variables that reside on the same cache line, leading to a degradation in performance. False sharing can be avoided by using padding or alignment to separate variables on different cache lines. What’s False Sharing?False sharing happens when threads modify variables that happen to live on the same cache line. The variables themselves are unrelated, but the cache line keeps bouncing between cores, invalidated over and over, and that’s what kills the performance. Feynman Method Imagine you and a colleague are sharing a single whiteboard, but you each only need one small corner of it. You’re writing your notes in the top-left corner. Your colleague is writing theirs in the top-right corner. You never touch each other’s work. Completely independent. But here’s the catch: the whiteboard can only be erased and rewritten one person at a time. Every time you want to write something, you have to claim the whole whiteboard, which means your colleague has to stop, wait for you to finish, then reclaim it before they can write again. And vice versa. Neither of you is doing anything wrong. You’re not interfering with each other’s content at all. But you’re constantly blocking each other from using the board, because the rule operates on the whole whiteboard, not on individual corners. That whiteboard is a cache line. Your corner is variable x. Your colleague’s corner is variable y. The “claim the whole board” rule is the MESI coherence protocol. The fix is simple: get a second whiteboard. Put your notes on one, your colleague’s notes on the other. Now you never have to wait for each other. That’s what alignas does, it forces each variable onto its own cache line, its own whiteboard, so the two cores never have to fight over the same one. Start with an ExampleConsider the following code snippet: 12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031323334353637383940414243444546474849505152#include <chrono>#include <cstdint>#include <iostream>#include <new>#include <thread>#include <vector>constexpr uint64_t kMaxTimes = 1000000000UL;#if 0 // X : bad examplestruct FalseSharing { volatile uint64_t x{0}; volatile uint64_t y{0};};#else// √ : good example, fixed the false-sharing issuestruct FalseSharing { alignas(64) volatile uint64_t x{0}; alignas(64) volatile uint64_t y{0};};#endifFalseSharing data;void WorkerA() { for (uint64_t i = 0; i < kMaxTimes; ++i) { ++data.x; }}void WorkerB() { for (uint64_t i = 0; i < kMaxTimes; ++i) { ++data.y; }}int main() { auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); std::thread t1(WorkerA); std::thread t2(WorkerB); t1.join(); t2.join(); auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); auto cost = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end - start); std::cout << "Time cost totally: " << cost.count() << " ms \n";} Building and running this gives: When false-sharing: When fixed: The performance result gap is significant, it costs 1776 ms to run the code snippet with false-sharing, while 409 ms to run it with fixed false-sharing issue.And it will be even worse if we run it on more cores. When reproducing the case by yourself, it should be noted that: We should compile with -O3, otherwise the compiler will optimize away the false-sharing issue. Sepecifically, it will simply remove the loop and add the final result. It was like “You nerd, why not add the variable all at once??”. We should use volatile to ensure that the compiler doesn’t optimize away the access to the variables in the example. Otherwise, the variable is cached in the CPU register, making it hard to observe the performance degradation. Since it optimizes away a ton of DRAM memory access. Under the HoodCPUs don’t read individual bytes from RAM. They read in fixed-size chunks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes on most modern x86 and ARM processors. When a core accesses any byte in memory, the entire 64-byte line containing it is pulled into L1 cache. This is usually a win. But in multithreaded code, it creates a trap. Suppose Thread A writes to x and Thread B writes to y. Different variables, different threads, no logical sharing. But if x and y sit within the same 64-byte cache line, the CPU doesn’t know that. Every time Thread A writes, it acquires exclusive ownership of the line, which invalidates Thread B’s copy. Thread B then reloads the line before it can write. Then A’s copy is invalidated. Back and forth, millions of times per second. This is false sharing: threads that don’t share data logically, but are forced by hardware to behave as if they do. The mechanism is the MESI cache coherence protocol. A write transitions a cache line to Modified on the writing core and broadcasts Invalid to all other cores holding a copy. Each invalidation costs dozens to hundreds of cycles and they never stop. SolutionMethod1: PaddingBy adding padding to the struct, we can separate the variables onto different cache lines, which avoids false sharing. In C++, we can use keyword alignas to align the variables. 123456// √ : good example, fixed the false-sharing issue// Usually 64 byte cache line, in C++17 `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` is the right answer.struct FixFalseSharing { alignas(64) volatile uint64_t x{0}; alignas(64) volatile uint64_t y{0};}; The padding happens during compilation phase by adding padding bit between the variables. Method2: Thread localAnother way to avoid false sharing is to use thread-local storage by rethinking the design if possible.By declaring the variables as thread-local, each thread gets its own copy of the variable, which avoids false sharing.It’s like: 1thread_local uint64_t x; // each process has its own version Caveats Padding wastes memory. A padded char occupies 64 bytes instead of 1, and for a large array of padded structs, that 8x memory bloat can hurt cache efficiency at a higher level than the false sharing you were fixing. 64 bytes is the common cache line size on x86/ARM today, but it isn’t universal. Prefer std::hardware_destructive_interference_size over hardcoding the number. True sharing is a different problem. If two threads genuinely need to access the same variable, padding does nothing, that’s a synchronisation problem, not a layout problem. To confirm false sharing is actually the cause, run perf stat -e cache-misses ./xxxx on Linux. A suspiciously high cache miss rate under the parallel workload is usually the tell. False sharing happens at every cache level, but it hurts worst at L1. Each core’s L1 and L2 are private, so when two cores write to variables on the same cache line, the coherence protocol keeps invalidating those private copies. The reloading core usually finds a valid copy in the shared L3 (about 40 cycles) instead of going all the way to RAM, since the contested line stays hot in the hierarchy from the other core’s writes. The cost isn’t the fetch distance, it’s how often the invalidation happens: a 4-cycle L1 hit turns into a 40-cycle L3 reload on every single write. Across NUMA sockets with no shared L3, it gets worse still. Key takeaway

posts.title: What's true understanding?
posts.text: Recently I’ve taken a class in UoA called “Self-Leadership”, which has given me a great deal of food for thought. It was somewhat novel and unfamiliar to me, and I mistook it for a typical self-success course.But the course content turned out to be surprisingly insightful. I’ve learned the most fundamental practice of self-leadership: reflection. There is no secret formula or magic behind it. It simply offers me a quiet chance to pause, slow down, and reflect on my inner self. TL;DR The illusion of understanding is a common trap in learning, where we feel like we understand something but lack genuine mastery. Use Feynman’s Method to check if you understand the concept. ObservationThese days I spent plenty of time diving into CSAPP, a classic book in computer science. Over the past few years in my work, I always intended to read this book thoroughly, but never got around to it. What I found interesting is that I acted differently. I somehow took on two distinct approaches once I began learning basic concepts such as Virtual Memory and Set Associative Caches. To summarize, I understand Set Associative Caches better than Virtual Memory. Meanwhile, reading the chapter on Virtual Memory felt more enjoyable and rewarding. In contrast, studying the other topic is quite challenging and “full of dopamine”. InflectionWhy?It is an issue with the illusion of understanding. It is recognition, yet not genuine mastery. When I closed the book, and looked back at the whole picture of Virtual Memory. I asked myself, but I got stuck over and over again. I couldn’t clarify the details of the concept, and I came up with some new questions. It ended up the knowledge is like a cyclone, it comes and goes, leaving a mess. I think the reason is that I used to use Virtual Memory a lot in my work. Therefore, I just read the concepts happily without stop thinking more about it. There was a voice in mind said “Yeah, that’s it. The layout is just like that. The underlying mechanism is just like that.”. I was so satisfied that I had learnt so much again. (Maybe after several days, I could be “happy” once more). 😔 In terms of Set Associative Caches, it’s not a huge knowledge, so I break it down into smaller parts and draw diagrams to help me understand it better. I somehow map the diagrams in my mind, and start explaining it to myself. Every time I get stuck by something that I can’t make it clear, I just go back to the book and read it again. Eventually, I really master it! I can spot connections between it and my existing knowledge. 😁 Implication && ActionI may have tried these methods consciously or unconsciously before. But now I need to define them clearly and supervise myself to see if I can put them into practice 👊. Thinking about how to articulate the ideas without opening the book. Actually it’s Feynman’s Method. Personally, I can understand about 90% of new knowledge after using the Feynman Method. Drawing diagrams to help me understand the concepts better. Break down the knowledge into smaller parts, making it easier to take action. AttachmentHere’s the Pros. and Cons. of using Feynman’s Method, just for you information.
